title: Central Bosnia: The Three-Way War
content:
No region of Bosnia-Herzegovina better illustrated the war's chaotic geometry than the central highlands. By mid-1993, the municipalities of Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, Kakanj, and their surrounding villages had become a patchwork of overlapping confrontation lines where three armies -- the ARBiH, the HVO, and the VRS -- fought simultaneously, sometimes within sight of each other's positions.

The geography of central Bosnia made partition along clean ethnic lines impossible. Bosniak and Croat villages alternated across the landscape in a pattern that no line on a map could separate without displacing tens of thousands of people. The VRS held the mountain ridges to the north and east, pressing inward. The HVO controlled clusters of Croat-majority towns -- Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak -- that sat like islands within broader ARBiH-controlled territory. The ARBiH held the larger population centers of Travnik, Zenica, and Kakanj but faced enemies on multiple fronts with inadequate supply lines running through contested terrain.

The eruption of the Croat-Bosniak war in April 1993 transformed this region from a shared defensive zone into a three-way battlefield. The ICTY Kordic Trial Judgment (IT-95-14/2-T) documented how HVO forces under the political direction of Dario Kordic launched offensives against Bosniak villages and neighborhoods in the Lasva Valley, seeking to consolidate Croat-claimed territory. The ARBiH response came in June 1993, when the 3rd Corps under General Enver Hadzihasanovic launched a counteroffensive that recaptured Travnik and expelled much of its Croat population -- an action that the ICTY Hadzihasanovic Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T) examined in the context of command responsibility for crimes committed by ARBiH subordinates.

The tactical situation in central Bosnia defied conventional military logic. HVO forces in Vitez and Busovaca were effectively surrounded by ARBiH territory but continued to resist, supplied through intermittent corridors and stockpiled reserves. The ARBiH 3rd Corps held the demographic advantage but was stretched across too many fronts, fighting the HVO to its south and west while maintaining positions against the VRS to the north and east. The VRS, for its part, exploited the Croat-Bosniak split by maintaining pressure on both forces while avoiding the costly urban combat that central Bosnia's terrain demanded.

The civilian consequences were devastating. Each offensive and counteroffensive produced waves of displacement. Bosniaks expelled from HVO-controlled areas fled toward Zenica and Travnik. Croats expelled from ARBiH-controlled areas moved toward Vitez, Kiseljak, or out of central Bosnia entirely. The result was a progressive demographic sorting that the prewar population distribution had made seem impossible -- achieved through violence, intimidation, and the destruction of homes that ensured no return.

The Kiseljak pocket presented a particularly acute example of the region's fragmentation. HVO forces there were entirely cut off from other Croat-held territory, connected to the outside world only through VRS-controlled corridors whose use depended on tacit Serb cooperation. This arrangement -- in which the HVO and VRS, nominally enemies, maintained functional agreements while both fought the ARBiH -- illustrated the war's shifting alliances at their most cynical.

Central Bosnia's three-way war continued through the autumn and winter of 1993, with no faction capable of achieving a decisive result. The Washington Agreement of March 1994 would end the Croat-Bosniak dimension of the fighting and create the Federation, but the months of combat had already transformed the region's demographic landscape in ways that no agreement could reverse.
